title: World action models vs VLAs: predict the video, or just the moves
description: Both look at a camera image, read an instruction and output robot moves. A VLA starts from an image-and-text model and learns the moves. A WAM starts from a video model and also learns the frames that come next. Eight drawings on what that changes.

title: Imprint: Memory Without Curation - Learning Multi-Stream Latent Memory for Robot Policies
description: Keep every stream, compress it as you go, and learn what to remember.

title: Offline empowerment: Learn where to explore from old data
description: Empowerment measured from unlabeled data guides online exploration.

title: Faster-WAM in LeRobot: from 300 cache reads to 10
description: Faster-WAM cuts a world action model's action expert to one layer. I added it to LeRobot behind opt-in flags and timed it on an A100 with random weights.

title: Policy gradients: fair credit and careful steps
description: Four ways a policy-gradient update can go wrong on a robot task: blaming actions for the past, rewarding every attempt, overshooting on reused data, and groups that teach nothing. Reward-to-go, baselines, PPO clipping and group advantages, with their limits.

title: Learning from a fixed dataset: missing actions and bad demonstrations
description: A fixed robot dataset can mislead a learner in two different ways: a hole, where it asks about actions nobody tried, and mistakes, where it copies bad demonstrations. Stay close to the data for the first, and weight actions by the reward for the second.

title: Mode averaging: two good routes, one bad average
description: Why copying demonstrations that go left and right around a box can send a robot into the box, and what flow policies and action chunks change.

title: Reinforcement learning: the problems behind the methods
description: Why I am learning reinforcement learning, and the six problems that drive its algorithms: delayed reward, exploration, waiting, scale, reusing data and feedback.

title: Foundations of value-based RL: a family tree and a Q table
description: One selected branch of RL, the value-based methods from the trial-and-error idea to DQN, where each later method fixes a problem an earlier one handles badly. Then Q-learning, which nudges one score toward the reward plus its best guess about the next cell.

title: ASPIRE: Can you zero-shot robotics with a coding agent?
description: ASPIRE lets a coding agent debug robot programs from execution traces and save each verified fix as a text skill. What the loop does, and what the numbers cover.

title: Bootstrapping: learn before the reward arrives
description: Why waiting for the final reward is slow, and how borrowing the next state's estimate lets you learn during the walk, with one worked update.

title: Function approximation: share a value, share an error
description: When states share a few weights, one update can teach states you never visited, and it can also blur two states together and move the target you're chasing.

title: On-policy and off-policy: whose future are we learning?
description: A value target has to assume what you do next: on-policy learning assumes the moves you actually make, and off-policy learning assumes a different policy's moves.

title: The deadly triad: how a guess can train itself upward
description: Function approximation, bootstrapping and off-policy data each make RL practical. Off-policy value learners such as deep Q-networks (DQN) and soft actor-critic (SAC) use all three, even though together they can let a prediction feed its own target with nothing to pull it back down.

title: Why can't robots remember?
description: Many robot policies decide from the last few frames. A snapshot of six ways to give them memory in October 2026, what each one stores, and what has been measured.

title: Recipes for choosing a learning target
description: Rules of thumb for a reinforcement learning target: freeze, take a second estimate, or take the minimum, and why the combinations table is one reading, not a law.

title: I made a small game where RL algorithms break
description: Breaking Bellman is a free browser game for learning reinforcement learning. Real algorithms train in your browser and fail, and you fix them one word at a time.

title: Teaching my drawing arm to keep learning
description: After part 6: direct motor drive, learning between drawings, feedback during a stroke, and a twin tested across days. The repeat floor is not a claim of one-millimeter control.

title: How do I get the XYZ position of my robot's tool tip?
description: I get $10,000 worth of measurements from a $40 drawing tablet. Now I want the height of the pen too.

title: Where the last millimeter of my drawing arm goes
description: My SO-101 arm cannot see its own pen tip. A tablet can. Here is what the tablet showed: how much error a learned correction removes, which causes are left, and why the base joint matters most.

title: EigenDEXplore: Teach a robot hand how to explore
description: Human motion guides its experiments. Every joint stays free.

title: A few predictions about robotics
description: If intelligence keeps getting cheaper, the robotics industry may start to look more like a combination of AI infrastructure, industrial services, and manufacturing.

title: Learning what the physics misses
description: Where a neural network fits in a robot controller. A network that learns only what the physics model gets wrong does the same job as a Kalman disturbance estimate, with more freedom, and this is where recent research is going.

title: A pen holder that shows the arm’s error, not its own
description: I want to see my SO-101 trajectory errors as ink on paper. For that, the pen must not add an error of its own. I made five holder designs. The one I release is a printed sleeve that slides onto the stock gripper: 4 printed parts, nothing to buy, any pen from 8 to 13 mm.

title: Six ways to choose the goal
description: One general formula for the goal sent to a servo. Every controller I built, from a plain look-ahead to MPC, is that formula with some terms set to zero.

title: Seeing finer than the sensor
description: The sensor side of the joint equation: why differences of encoder ticks explode the noise, and how an observer or a Kalman filter can estimate an angle finer than one tick.

title: One equation, and every way the arm misses it
description: Start from torque = inertia × acceleration, then add each term a cheap servo arm really has: gravity, friction, a payload, dead time, a dead band. Each term is one way the arm misses its target.

title: How robot control is changing
description: From copying a person to practicing and imagining: how a robot chooses its next movement in 2026, and what is still missing.

title: Why I am learning robotics
description: The most impressive robots of the last decade stayed in videos because they could not generalize. Language models changed that, and robotics now looks like language models in 2019.

title: How an arm moves: joints, geometry, and motor control
description: From encoder readings to gripper position: a visual guide to robot geometry, servos, and the commands that connect them.
